chunks: "Embedded systems are everywhere, and the common pattern is a small computer dedicated to one job, reading sensors and driving something.
At home: a microwave oven, a washing machine, a thermostat, a TV remote, a smart speaker. In a car: dozens of ECUs: engine control, ABS, airbag, power windows, infotainment.
Industrial: PLCs, motor drives, robot controllers, building automation. Medical: pacemakers, insulin pumps, glucose meters, infusion pumps.
Communication: routers, modems, base stations. Aerospace and hobby: drone flight controllers, satellites, 3D printers. The useful way to compare them is by what constrains them.
A pacemaker is ultra-low power and safety-critical: it has to run for years on a small battery and never fail.
An airbag or ABS controller is hard real-time: the deadline is milliseconds, and a missed deadline is a failure, not a slowdown.
A TV remote is cost-driven, a fraction of a dollar of silicon. A router is throughput-driven, so it uses a microprocessor running Linux.

One I could describe in detail is an engine controller: it reads crank position, air flow and temperature, and has to fire the spark within about 28 microseconds per degree of crank angle at 6000 rpm."
